Rate each account from 1 (not valuable for this study) to 7 (highly valuable for this study).

A. A system in the left half of the brain readily generates confident explanations for actions, feelings and bodily states, including ones it did not initiate. On this account that system is the whole source of the self: the sense of being an I is entirely the running explanation it produces to make behavior appear unified and intended. The I seems to continue because the system keeps fitting each new action and feeling into the same explanatory account of who is acting.

B. The brain continuously anticipates the state of its own body, especially internal signals such as heartbeat and breathing, and combines these anticipations into a representation of the whole organism. The sense of being an I arises from this representation, which is not experienced as a representation, so the system simply experiences itself as someone. The I seems to continue because relatively stable general expectations about the organism organize changing bodily and perceptual signals over time.

C. Pure awareness, an unchanging witness, is one's true self. The sense of being a particular I, a doer and experiencer with this body and mind, arises through an I-making function, when the witness and the body and mind are mistakenly identified, the properties of each being attributed to the other. The personal I changes; what truly continues is the unchanging witness with which it is mistakenly identified, present through waking, dreaming and deep sleep.

D. What is ordinarily taken to be a person can be analyzed into five changing groups of processes: the body, feeling, perception, mental habits and consciousness. None is a self, but through wanting and holding on, each is repeatedly taken as "this is mine, this I am, this is my self." The sense of being an I comes from this appropriation, including a subtle sense of "I am" that can persist even after belief in a self is abandoned. The I seems to continue because this claiming keeps recurring.

E. Alongside the ordinary forms of sensory and mental awareness runs a largely subliminal stream of consciousness, which carries traces of past actions and experiences as latent tendencies that later give rise to new experience. A further mental function continuously takes this stream to be a self, accompanied by a view of self, self-regard, self-attachment and self-confusion. The sense of being an I arises from this constant, largely unnoticed misidentification. The I seems to continue because this stream flows on without ever being a fixed self.

When attention is turned directly toward it, this thought can be seen to arise and pass like any other, and experience no longer seems organized around a separate owner. The I seems to continue only because the thought recurs so often that the gaps between its appearances go unnoticed.

G. People continuously weave their actions, memories and plans into stories, and the I is the main character these stories are organized around. Like a balance point, it is a useful abstraction rather than a physical part of anything. The sense of being an I arises from this storytelling activity, much of which occurs without deliberate authorship. The I seems to continue because the story is constantly extended and revised so that new events are told as happening to the same character.

Every conscious experience is lived from the inside, with a built-in first-person character, before any reflection, self-image or story about oneself. This is the most basic I. None is a self, but through craving and clinging each is repeatedly taken as "this is mine, this I am, this is my self." The sense of being an I comes from this appropriation, including a subtle conceit, "I am," that can persist even after belief in a self is abandoned. The I seems to continue because I-making keeps recurring.

D. Advaita Vedānta account of ahaṃkāra and ātman
Pure consciousness, the witness, is unchanging and is one's true self. The sense of being a particular I, a doer and experiencer with this body and mind, arises through the I-maker, when the witness and the body-mind are mistakenly identified through superimposition. At the most basic, moment-to-moment level, its continuity comes from the temporal structure of consciousness: each present moment retains the just-past and anticipates the about-to-come, so experience is lived as one flow.

On this account the interpreter is the whole source of the self: the sense of being an I is entirely the running explanation it produces to make behavior appear unified and intended. The I seems to continue because the interpreter keeps fitting each new action and feeling into the same explanatory account of who is acting.
